title: NetBSD 11.0 Ships First Stable RISC-V Port and Ten-Millisecond Boot Kernel - Tech Times
content:
The NetBSD Project shipped NetBSD 11.0 on August 1, 2026, delivering the first BSD operating system with an officially supported, stable 64-bit RISC-V port — completing a development cycle that spanned seven release candidates and more than eighteen months since the prior stable release, as announced by developer Martin Husemann on the project's official blog. The nineteenth major release of one of the oldest continuously developed open-source operating systems also debuts a kernel variant that boots a full virtual machine in roughly 10 milliseconds on 2020-era hardware, and adds twelve new Linux-compatible system calls that substantially expand the range of pre-built Linux binaries the system can run without modification. For developers building on RISC-V hardware, the release represents something the embedded-development community has not had before: a production-quality Unix-like operating system licensed under permissive BSD terms — no ISA licensing fees, no copyleft obligations — running on a royalty-free open-hardware instruction set architecture. The combination is the first fully permissive-license OS stack on open-hardware silicon with official vendor distributions, as RISC-V International explains in its description of the open standard architecture. NetBSD 11.0 marks the first stable release to include an official binary distribution for 64-bit RISC-V platforms, as detailed in the NetBSD 11.0 release notes. The supported hardware lineup centers on boards built around the StarFive JH7110 system-on-chip — specifically the VisionFive 2 single-board computer and the PINE64 STAR64 — with more basic bring-up (GPIO and UART serial console) for the Allwinner D1 SoC used on the MangoPi MQ Pro. QEMU is also fully supported for RISC-V virtualization, including Google Goldfish RTC, VirtIO networking, disk, and audio, making it practical for developers who want to target the architecture without dedicated hardware. The JH7110 implementation goes deeper than basic boot. The 11.0 RISC-V port supports PCI and PCIe devices, a True Random Number Generator, pin control, temperature sensors, and the in-kernel crash(8) debugger — the last item a reliable signal that the project treats this port as a development-ready target rather than a technology preview. The Allwinner D1 support remains more limited, reflecting the SoC's less mature Linux ecosystem that NetBSD's bring-up work has only partially replicated at this stage. RISC-V is an open-standard instruction set architecture developed at the University of California, Berkeley, managed by RISC-V International, a Swiss standards body with more than 4,500 member organizations across 70 countries. Unlike x86 (Intel) or Arm, which require design licenses, RISC-V is royalty-free and unencumbered — any company or developer can design, manufacture, and sell RISC-V chips without paying licensing fees. Combined with NetBSD's BSD license, the full hardware-to-OS stack now carries no proprietary licensing requirements anywhere in the chain. For x86 and amd64 users running virtual machines, 11.0 introduces a dedicated MICROVM kernel variant that boots a full NetBSD guest in approximately 10 milliseconds on hardware from around 2020, as documented in the NetBSD 11.0 release notes. That figure puts it in the territory of purpose-built unikernel-style systems — except MICROVM is a complete NetBSD environment, not a stripped-down single-application runtime. The engineering behind this number is specific. A traditional VM boot requires the hypervisor to emulate a complete PC firmware path: BIOS initialization, then PCI bus enumeration (which scans every possible device slot, a process that can add 100 milliseconds or more to startup time), then ACPI table parsing, before the OS kernel even begins loading. MICROVM eliminates all of that by combining three techniques. First, it uses PVH (Para-Virtual Hardware) boot — a protocol originally developed in the Xen virtualization project that bypasses the BIOS/ACPI firmware layer entirely, handing control directly to the OS kernel with a minimal hardware description. Second, it uses VirtIO MMIO (Memory-Mapped I/O) for device discovery rather than PCI. VirtIO is the de facto standard for paravirtualized VM I/O, maintained by OASIS; the MMIO variant discovers devices through memory-mapped register reads rather than a PCI configuration space scan. Third, NetBSD's new pv(4) pseudo-bus handles device attachment for VirtIO MMIO devices whose parameters are passed via the kernel command line — entirely bypassing the conventional bus enumeration framework. The net result: the VM kernel sees a minimal hardware description, finds its devices immediately through a command-line list rather than a bus scan, and reaches a running state in a fraction of the time a conventional VM requires. Non-Xen PVH boot is also supported more broadly in 11.0, enabling the qemu -kernel invocation path that many embedded-development workflows rely on. NetBSD's compat_linux(8) subsystem — a kernel-mode compatibility layer that allows Linux ELF binaries to execute on NetBSD without recompilation — received its largest expansion in years with 11.0. The twelve new or enhanced system calls include: epoll (implemented on top of the native kqueue mechanism), inotify filesystem event notifications, clone3, statx, readahead, close_range, waitid, renameat2, sync_file_range, syncfs, and POSIX message queues via the mq_* family, as listed in the release notes. A new memfd_create(2) system call — compatible with its Linux counterpart — was also added. The architectural note about epoll is worth pausing on. Linux's epoll is a scalable I/O event notification mechanism that lets applications monitor thousands of file descriptors efficiently, introduced in Linux 2.5.45 in 2002. NetBSD's kqueue does the same job — and more: kqueue handles file descriptors, processes, timers, filesystem events, and signals through a single unified API, while epoll is file-descriptor-only. Implementing epoll semantics on top of kqueue is architecturally clean precisely because kqueue is the more general system; the translation uses kqueue's EVFILT_READ and EVFILT_WRITE filters to satisfy epoll's narrower contract. Linux applications that were previously incompatible because they relied on epoll can now run on NetBSD using the same binary, without the application knowing anything has changed. The procfs pseudo-filesystem also gained sysvipc and self/limits entries specifically to improve process-introspection compatibility with Linux applications. The npf(7) packet filter — NetBSD's native, SMP-scalable firewall designed for parallel operation across multiple CPU cores — gained two notable capabilities in 11.0, documented in the release notes. Layer 2 filtering extends npf's reach below the IP layer, allowing forwarding decisions based on Ethernet-level information including MAC addresses and EtherType fields. This extends npf from a purely IP-layer traffic management tool into bridge and switch scenarios where decisions need to happen at the link layer. User and group-based filtering lets administrators write rules keyed to the UID or GID of the process originating a connection — enabling per-application or per-user firewall policies at the kernel level without external tooling. Beyond RISC-V, the hardware compatibility additions in 11.0 span from brand-new silicon to decades-old game consoles. Initial support for Qualcomm's Snapdragon X Elite platform includes the Oryon CPU cores, battery and charger sensor drivers, GPIO, and I2C controllers — giving NetBSD a foothold on the class of Arm-based PC hardware that has gained significant attention in the laptop market, as the release notes confirm. Read more:
FreeBSD Builds BSD-Native NTSYNC Driver, Launches AMD ROCm Compute Port The Nintendo Wii port — long a community showcase for NetBSD's extreme portability — received a substantial refresh: DVD drive support, a bwi(4) WLAN driver, USB Gecko serial console, hardware AES acceleration (used to speed disk encryption and Wi-Fi), an independent bootloader, and improved X.Org performance with GX RGB-to-YUY2 video conversion acceleration. A new virt68k port debuted, targeting Motorola 68000 emulation in QEMU through paravirtualized devices — providing a clean development and testing target for the m68k family of platforms without requiring physical vintage hardware. The NetBSD team was direct in the release announcement about a decision that will draw attention from any security-conscious reader: NetBSD 11.0 shipped knowing three security issues were unresolved. The three issues are: a missing local privilege check in hdaudio(4) ioctl commands (the workaround is straightforward — remove /dev/hdaudio* devices; audio remains functional); a remotely triggerable null pointer dereference in ipfilter (ipfilter is not included in any released kernel by default); and a use-after-free in pf's fragment reassembly code (pf is deprecated and also absent from released kernels by default). The practical risk to users running standard release kernels is limited, but the issues exist. Martin Husemann's explanation in the announcement is candid and points to a structural shift across the open-source security landscape: AI tools have accelerated vulnerability discovery to a pace where clean security slates before release may no longer be achievable. The FreeBSD Foundation made the same problem explicit in June 2026 when it launched a $250,000 AI-Assisted Vulnerability Discovery Project funded by the Linux Foundation's Alpha-Omega initiative, noting that AI tools had already reduced the effective time to exploitation to zero days for some open-source codebases. Security research firm Praetorian published a detailed account the same month of an AI agent that found multiple vulnerabilities in the FreeBSD kernel, including one that became CVE-2026-3038, illustrating the broader vulnerability-discovery pressure facing the BSD ecosystem. The team committed to pushing fixes into the stable branch shortly after the 11.0 release and is targeting a NetBSD 11.1 release within approximately two months. The third-party component refresh is extensive. OpenSSH moves to 10.3 — with DSA key support removed, so users with custom sshd_config configurations enabling DSA should audit their files before upgrading, per the release notes. OpenSSL updates to 3.5.7, GCC to 12.5.0, GDB to 15.1, tmux to 3.6b, and Xorg to 21.1.24. On the kernel performance side, virtio(4) drivers are now marked MPSAFE, meaning they no longer hold the big kernel lock and can execute in parallel across CPU cores, as the release notes document. The initial TCP retransmission timeout was reduced from 3 seconds to 1 second, in line with RFC 6298 — improving responsiveness on connections to slow or unresponsive peers. The igc(4) Intel Ethernet driver gained TCP Segmentation Offload support, and rge(4) now covers Realtek's RTL8126 5 Gbps parts. A new heartbeat(9) kernel mechanism uses hard interrupts to monitor soft interrupt processing and cross-CPU progress — the kernel equivalent of a watchdog, designed to catch situations where one CPU is silently failing to make forward progress. NetBSD's long tradition of standards conformance continues in 11.0 with enhanced compliance against both POSIX.1-2024 (Issue 8) and the C23 programming language standard, per the release notes. The libpthread library received an audit of missing cancellation points. The sh(1) shell adjusted tilde expansion to meet Issue 8 requirements. expr(1) now uses multibyte code points for the ":" and "length" operations as POSIX mandates. lint(1) gained C23 support. A new c17(1) compiler wrapper script was added as required by POSIX.1-2024. Installation images for all supported architectures are available from the NetBSD 11.0 CDN. The project recommends .img files for flash-based media such as USB drives, and these must be decompressed before flashing. DVD ISO images are preferred when CD-ROM size constraints are not a factor. Pre-configured ARM images with U-Boot are available from armbsd.org, and RISC-V images can be downloaded directly from the CDN. NetBSD 11.0 officially supports 64-bit RISC-V on the StarFive JH7110 SoC, used in the VisionFive 2 single-board computer (widely available for roughly $55–79) and the PINE64 STAR64 boards. QEMU virtualization for RISC-V is also fully supported, enabling development without dedicated hardware. The port includes the in-kernel crash(8) debugger and PCIe support, both indicators that the project treats this as a development-ready, not experimental, platform. The Allwinner D1 (MangoPi MQ Pro) has more limited support covering only GPIO and UART at this stage. For developers building embedded applications or evaluating BSD on open-hardware silicon, 11.0 represents the first stable, officially distributed starting point — not a preview release. The MICROVM kernel achieves its 10-millisecond boot time by eliminating the two most expensive phases of conventional VM startup: BIOS/ACPI firmware initialization and PCI bus enumeration. It uses PVH (Para-Virtual Hardware) boot — a protocol that hands control directly to the OS kernel with a minimal hardware description — and discovers its VirtIO devices through kernel command-line parameters rather than a PCI bus scan. Unikernels (such as MirageOS or Unikraft) can boot in under a millisecond but give up full OS generality; they run a single application, not a general-purpose Unix environment. MICROVM achieves 10ms while remaining a complete NetBSD system capable of running arbitrary software. Compared to a default Linux VM under QEMU, which typically takes several hundred milliseconds to boot, 10ms is a meaningful engineering achievement within the same class of host compatibility. The project made a deliberate trade-off: rather than delaying the release again while new issues continued to surface — a pattern the team attributed explicitly to AI-assisted vulnerability scanning tools that have accelerated discovery across the BSD ecosystem — the project chose to ship with full disclosure. The three open issues all have important mitigations: the hdaudio(4) privilege gap has a simple workaround (removing the device node), and the ipfilter and pf issues affect components not included in any released kernel by default. Users running standard release kernels from the CDN face limited practical exposure. Fixes are expected in the stable branch shortly after 11.0 and will ship with NetBSD 11.1, targeted approximately two months after this release. The twelve new Linux-compatible system calls in 11.0 — including epoll, inotify, clone3, and statx — close gaps that previously prevented many pre-built Linux ELF binaries from running on NetBSD at all. epoll in particular is used by a wide range of high-performance networked applications and event-driven frameworks; its absence was a meaningful compatibility barrier. The implementation is architecturally clean: NetBSD maps epoll semantics onto its native kqueue mechanism, which is the more general of the two APIs. A developer who has pre-built Linux binaries — including server software, language runtimes, and CLI tools — is likely to find meaningfully better compatibility against NetBSD 11.0 than against any prior release, without recompiling from source. ⓒ 2026 TECHTIMES.com All rights reserved. The intrinsic value estimate sits close to the market price, while earnings based multiples lean rich. Visa delivered 8.7% returns over the last year. See how this stacks up to the rest of the Diversified Financial industry. Visa has a book value of $18.87 per share and an average forecast return on equity of 71.61%, which feeds into a stable EPS estimate of $14.86 per share. With a cost of equity of $1.50 per share, the model calculates an excess return of $13.36 per share and a stable book value of $20.75 per share. Those inputs translate into an intrinsic value estimate of $383.86 per share, which is about 4.6% above the current share price. The recent plan to cut about 7% of the workforce to fund AI and payment growth initiatives helps explain why the market is still comfortable paying close to that Excess Returns estimate. On this Excess Returns view, Visa stock appears roughly fairly valued, with only a modest implied discount to intrinsic value. title: Alice V Wager Obituary - Orange County Register
content: Alice V. Wager passed away peacefully on July 19, 2026. She was 96 years old. Born Alice Valencia on March 5, 1930, in Orange, California, Alice was the eldest of five children of Ambrosio and Margarita (Borboa) Valencia. She grew up with her siblings Henry, Eva, Herbert, and Teresa on an orange grove in Irvine, where the family lived, and her father served as foreman. When Alice was 21, her father passed away. Her mother later married Alice’s stepfather, Roger Valencia. Alice graduated from Tustin High School, where she played field hockey. She formed many enduring friendships during those years and continued to see several of her high school friends well into her 90s. In 1951, while Alice was working in the ticket booth in front of the Fox West Coast Theatre in downtown Santa Ana, a small group of young Marines stationed at Marine Corps Air Station El Toro stopped by and struck up a conversation. Among them was Harry Dale Wager, Jr., from the suburbs of Chicago, who was bold enough to ask Alice out. Alice and Dale were married on March 18, 1952, and shared more than 40 years of marriage before his death in 1995. During the early years of their marriage, Alice and Dale moved back and forth from California to Tennessee while Dale served in the Marine Corps. They eventually settled in Santa Ana, California, where they built their life together and raised eight children–six sons and two daughters. Their home was filled with the challenges and laughter, chaos and peace, and love that comes with a large family. Alice devoted her life to raising her children and caring for her family. She later helped support the family working as a baker at the local high school, where some of her children and plenty of their friends would stop by the cafeteria for the cookies, corners of cake, and other desserts she had set aside for them. She also drove the little bus for Bailey’s Young World, transporting young dancers to lessons. She was a wonderful cook who prepared meals not only for her large family, but also for anyone else who happened to show up. There was always room for one more at the Wager home. You considered yourself lucky if you had an authentic Mexican meal prepared by Alice. A gifted seamstress, she made clothing, costumes, and countless other creations for her children and grandchildren. She loved crocheting, making unique baby blankets and Christmas stockings. Many of those stockings are still hung on mantels or draped over sofas every year. She enjoyed crafts of all kinds and passed her love of creating to her children. Alice also loved to garden, and her patio was always filled with beautiful flowers she tended to with great care. She always knew exactly what each plant or flower needed to thrive. Some of her children now carry on her love of gardening in their own homes. Alice was beautiful, strong, smart, funny, and devoted. She was endlessly curious, listening with genuine interest, wanting to know what others were doing and thinking. She had a playful and joyous spirit, was never afraid to be silly, and continued learning throughout her life. She played a mean game of Scrabble and Canasta, and was a devoted fan of her beloved Los Angeles Dodgers, rarely missing an opportunity to watch or listen to a game. Everyone was welcome in Alice’s home. Friends of her children still remember the meals, care, and sense of belonging she offered them while they were growing up. To many, she was like a second mother. Alice was never judgmental or unkind. She accepted people as they were and met them with patience, understanding, and an open heart. Throughout her life, her Catholic faith remained important to her, and she was active in her parish. After Dale’s death, Alice moved in with her mother and stepfather and cared for them until their deaths. For a time, Alice lived with her son, Doug, along with his wife, Kerry, and their two daughters. She found great joy surrounded by all of her grandchildren and great-grandchildren. She attended as many of their events, milestones, and celebrations as she could, was happiest when her family was gathered together, and to the very end, was overjoyed when she had a baby on her lap. Whether they called her Grandma, Granny, Wow, Gigi, GG, or Grandma Alice, each of her grandchildren and great-grandchildren held a special place in her heart. She had boundless energy and, true to her generous spirit, continued cooking for and entertaining her growing family well into her later years. Although Alzheimer’s took much from her in her last few years, she remained strong until her last day. She was lovingly and devotedly cared for by her daughter Donna during the last three years of her life, and passed away peacefully and comfortably at home. Alice’s greatest legacy is the unconditional love, kindness, and devotion she gave so freely, which helped shape the beautiful family she leaves behind: 8 children, 18 grandchildren, and 12 great-grandchildren. While heartbroken, each knew they were so very loved. She was so deeply loved in return and will be terribly missed. She will always be remembered as the heart and soul of the family. Alice is survived by her eight children: Sharon (Rich) Wood, Steve (Pat) Wager, Art (Denise) Wager, Alan (Laurie) Wager, Roy (Michelle) Wager, Donna Wager, Mick (Lisa) Wager, and Doug (Kerry) Wager. She is also survived by her 18 grandchildren: Edwin (Jennifer) Fryslie, Kristen (Tom) Morales, Brian (Christy) Wager, Blake Wager, Kelly (Matt Goode) Wager, Sarah (Ben) Zitney, Lindsay (Brad) Ormonde, Jordan (Anthony) Sannipoli, Jake (Alex) Wager, Jack Wager, David (Amanda) Wager, Abby Wager, Dylan Wager, Dustin Wager, Claire Wager, Anna Wager, Marina Wager, and Elisa Wager; and her 12 great-grandchildren: Lola, Landon, Sophia, Ben, Finley, Avery, Theo, Arlo, Nico, Nolan, Stella, and Rylan. She is also survived by her sister, Eva (Robert) Himmerich, and many nieces, nephews, cousins, and extended family members. Alice was preceded in death by her husband, Harry Dale Wager Jr.; her parents, Ambrosio and Margarita “Margaret” Valencia; her stepfather, Roger Valencia; her brothers, Henry and Herbert Valencia; and her sister, Teresa. A Mass of Christian Burial will be held at 10:30 a.m. on Tuesday, August 4, 2026, at St. Irenaeus Catholic Church in Cypress, California. A private interment will take place at a later date at Riverside National Cemetery. In lieu of flowers, please consider making a donation to a charity of your choice. The family would like to thank Sabrina Huizar, who walked beside Mom over the past two years–along with Tracy Benny, Melissa and Kris from Seniors Helping Seniors, and our friends at Silverado Hospice–all of whom served Mom with such skill, sensitivity, and compassion. title: Stan V Lowe Obituary - Moraga (1930-2026) - eastbaytimes.com
content: At the age of 96, Stan V. Lowe left us. He passed away peacefully and on his own terms on July 23rd, in his beloved home of fifty years, surrounded by love and admiration from family and friends for his life well-lived. Born Sanford Vernon Lowenstein on April 12, 1930 to loving parents, Jacob and Mollie Lowenstein, Stan was a proud native Oaklander. After the untimely death of his father at age 42, Mollie sold their Oakland pharmacy and their home on Vernon Street and moved with young Stan and her two sisters to Los Angeles to take jobs in an airplane factory preparing for the war effort shortly before the start of WWII. In order to avoid the taunts and bullying of Stan’s school mates, Mollie legally changed their surname to Lowe. In 1944, they returned to Oakland where Stan enrolled at Oakland High School and graduated in the class of 1948. Stan attended Golden Gate College in San Francisco while working at the Richmond and Marin shipyards until his graduation with a bachelor’s degree in business administration in 1951. After serving two years in the Army as an auditor at various military installations in the Mid-West, Stan happily returned to Oakland to earn his CPA license and start his decades long career as a certified public accountant. He and his friend and associate, Tom Tripodes, together formed their partnership in Tripodes and Lowe, Certified Public Accountants in San Francisco. A few years later they joined Tom’s friends in the Greek community to found Olympic Savings and Loan with branches throughout the Bay Area. The business was later sold to Home Savings and Loan. Stan was a forty-year member of the California Society of Certified Public Accountants. He also held memberships in the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants and the Commonwealth Club. While visiting a client, Stan met Barbara Huebel, the bookkeeper who captured his heart. The couple spent the next 48 years together, first in Montclair, then in Moraga. They had decided to raise and show Corgis as a hobby, and the home in Moraga was on a large property perfect for the dogs to romp together and enjoy the mild climate. Stan and Barbara later also enjoyed entertaining family and friends in their vacation home in Incline Village, fishing in the Sierra Mountain lakes, wagering in local and Las Vegas casinos, showing their championship Corgis at dog shows in the U.S. and Canada, and traveling the world. Sadly, Barbara passed away in 2006, leaving Stan a bachelor again, in the company of his beloved dogs. Stan kept fit by jogging the trails of Lamorinda and working out with his friend and personal trainer, Katie Ross. After the death of his last Corgi in 2009, Katie introduced her friend’s mother, Carolyn Tamony, the widowed mother of ten adult children. As an only child with no children himself, Stan was somewhat intimidated by Carolyn’s large family. But attraction won out and they found each other to be loving companions over the next 16 years, the happiest of his life as Stan often proclaimed. He introduced Carolyn to the pleasure of a winning hand at the casinos and choosing the winner at the horse races. She updated the interior of his home and transformed his large backyard into a lovely garden, where they sat in the warm, shaded patio, relaxed, and listened to Frank Sinatra, the Mills Brothers, and the Big Band melodies. Stan loved watching the Forty-Niners, the SF Giants, Golden State Warriors, Stanford women’s basketball, and, lately, the Valkyries. When there was no sports to entertain him, he enjoyed the old movies of the 30’s, 40’s and 50’s, remembering the names of not only the stars but the myriad of character actors as well. Grieving Stan’s loss are his cousins, Randy Strom and his partner Lorrie Yates, Janet Rosenfeld and her family, Mardee Strom, Gay Strom Schrag, and Judy Strom Norrshen and husband Larry. Also grieving are Barbara’s son Bob Huebel, his wife Barbara and son Ryan, as well as dear friends Jeff Elfont, Katie Ross, and Maria and Bruce Peuse, and all of Carolyn’s children and grandchildren, and most especially Carolyn, who will miss his twinkling blue eyes, his warm smile and hearty laughter, his singing the old standards of his youth, and his silly Oakland High jokes. The family thanks Sinai Memorial Chapel in Lafayette for the funeral arrangements. Stan was interred on July 29 next to Barbara in a private ceremony at Home of Eternity Cemetery in Oakland. title: FRANKLIN: Ann V. Taschereau - Franklin Observer
content: Ann (Rofino) Taschereau, a lifelong Franklin resident, passed away peacefully on Friday, July 31, 2026 surrounded by the love of family. Born December 24, 1931 in Franklin, MA, she was the daughter of the late Joseph Rofino and Grazia (Grillo) Rofino and beloved wife of the late Lionel "Leo" Taschereau, with whom she shared 66 years of marriage. Ann held multiple jobs throughout her life, including owning her own restaurant, "Ann's Kitchen" with her husband, located in Franklin. Her favorite role however, was as a homemaker. She enjoyed cooking not only for family and friends, but whenever she met someone new, she always tried to invite them over to cook for them. Being Italian, she was known for her great cooking skills including her famous meatballs. Everyone also looked forward to receiving her Pizzelles during the holidays. She was full of zest and made everyone around her laugh. Her charisma will be sorely missed by all. Ann is survived by her granddaughter, Sarah Larsen and her son-in-law, Mark Bulen of Franklin. She is predeceased by her daughter, JoAnn (Taschereau) Bulen. Family and friends are invited to attend her funeral on Thursday, August 6th at 9am from the Charles F. Oteri & Son Franklin Funeral Home, 33 Cottage St. followed by a funeral Mass at 10am in St. Mary's Parish, 1 Church Square Franklin, MA. To view the Mass stmarysfranklin.org Internment will follow at St. Mary's Cemetery, Franklin. Calling hours are Wednesday, August 5th from 4pm to 7pm at the funeral home. Sunny, with a high of 91 and low of 70 degrees. Partly Cloudy in the morning, sunny during the afternoon, mist overnight.

By adding that detail, it’s not a hint that I particularly dislike the fella or anything like that; he just reminds me of the position we were in. Unless anything crazy happens in the future, I doubt he will manage a bigger club than ourselves, and anyone in his position would have had a go at it, but it was always too big for him. title: The Most Reliable Harley-Davidson V-Twin Ever Built - Top Speed
content: Harley-Davidson has built more than a few V-twin engines with reputations for going the distance. The modern Milwaukee-Eight has quickly earned riders' trust, while the Twin Cam and Evolution continue to inspire fierce loyalty decades after their introductions. Each has a legitimate claim in the reliability conversation, but one stands apart for reasons that go beyond engineering alone. To understand why, it's worth looking at what each engine got right and what ultimately separates the winner from the rest. If this debate were based only on modern engineering, the     Milwaukee-Eight would have a strong claim to the title. Introduced for the 2017 model year, it marked Harley-Davidson's biggest Big Twin redesign in nearly two decades, delivering smoother performance, better cooling, and fewer vibrations than the Twin Cam it replaced. The improvements weren't just about increasing power. Harley also focused on creating an engine that felt more comfortable and confidence-inspiring for everyday riding. A four-valve cylinder head improved efficiency, while refinements to the engine's design reduced vibration without sacrificing the unmistakable feel of a Harley     V-twin. The result was an engine that made long days in the saddle noticeably easier without feeling disconnected from the brand's traditional character. Just as importantly, the     Milwaukee-Eight has earned a reputation for reliability. Thousands of owners have logged impressive mileage with little more than routine maintenance, and the platform has proven itself in everything from     daily commuters to cross-country touring motorcycles. That's an impressive accomplishment for an engine that also produces noticeably more power than the Twin Cam before it. For riders buying a new Harley-Davidson, it's easy to see why so many choose the Milwaukee-Eight today. It delivers the refinement many riders wanted without losing the     character that has always defined a Harley V-twin. It may even become the answer to this question one day. For now, the Milwaukee-Eight is missing one thing no amount of engineering can accelerate: decades of real-world proof. To find the engine that built Harley-Davidson's reputation for long-term durability, you have to look a little further back. When Harley-Davidson introduced the     Twin Cam for the 1999 model year, it had big shoes to fill. Replacing the well-regarded Evolution was never going to be easy, but the new engine brought meaningful improvements in power, torque, and refinement while quickly earning a loyal following of its own. Over the years, the Twin Cam found its way into everything from Dynas and Softails to Electra Glides and Road Kings. Owners appreciated its stronger performance and relaxed highway manners, and many examples have accumulated well into six-figure mileage with nothing more than scheduled service. Whether crossing states or     commuting every day, the Twin Cam built its reputation the same way every dependable engine does: by quietly accumulating miles year after year. For all its strengths, the Twin Cam never completely escaped one well-known issue: the early cam chain tensioners. On 1999–2006 models, the spring-loaded tensioner shoes could wear faster than expected, and if left unchecked, they had the potential to cause expensive engine damage. Harley later introduced hydraulic tensioners that greatly improved durability, and many earlier bikes have since been upgraded, but the issue remains part of the engine's legacy. That single weakness is what keeps the Twin Cam from taking the top spot. Without it, there's a strong argument that Harley's second-generation Big Twin could have become the company's undisputed     reliability champion. Instead, the title still belongs to an engine that earned its reputation with fewer caveats. Long before the Twin Cam arrived, Harley had already built a V-twin that owners trusted to rack up hundreds of thousands of miles with remarkably few known trouble spots. By the time the     Evolution arrived for the 1984 model year, Harley-Davidson had something to prove. Earlier V-twins had earned devoted followings, but they had also developed a reputation for oil leaks, frequent maintenance, and inconsistent reliability. The Evolution 1340 Big Twin didn't just replace the     Shovelhead; it transformed how riders viewed Harley-Davidson reliability. The Evolution Sportster engine also built an impressive reputation for durability, but the Evolution 1340 is the engine that redefined reliability for Harley-Davidson's Big Twin lineup. Unlike the engines before it, the Evolution was designed to solve many of the durability complaints riders had simply accepted as part of owning a Harley. Aluminum cylinders and heads improved heat dissipation, hydraulic lifters reduced routine maintenance, and the straightforward design avoided the kind of chronic weak points that plagued some earlier V-twins. It wasn't the most powerful V-twin Harley had ever built, but emphasizing durability over chasing     bigger horsepower numbers became one of its greatest strengths. Owners found they could ride farther, wrench less, and trust the engine to keep delivering mile after mile. Plenty of Harley engines have earned loyal fans. The Evolution earned something even more valuable: time. Four decades after its debut, countless examples have surpassed 100,000 miles, with many reaching 200,000 miles or more while requiring little beyond routine maintenance and timely repairs. That kind of     longevity isn't built on marketing claims or a few standout examples; it's backed by millions of miles accumulated by everyday riders. The Milwaukee-Eight may eventually earn the same distinction, and a well-maintained Twin Cam can be an     exceptionally dependable engine in its own right. However, the Evolution stands apart because it transformed Harley-Davidson's reputation while proving its durability over decades of real-world use. That's why, when the conversation turns to the most reliable Harley-Davidson V-twin ever built, the Evolution still sets the standard. But earning a legendary reputation is only half the equation. Whether an Evolution-powered Harley is still a smart motorcycle to buy decades later is a different question entirely. The Evolution's reputation wasn't left behind when production ended. One reason Evo-powered Harleys remain so desirable is that they occupy a unique place in Harley-Davidson history. They're modern enough to live with comfortably, yet simple enough that many owners still do much of     their own maintenance. That balance has become increasingly rare as motorcycles have added more electronics, sensors, and rider-assistance technology. Replacement parts remain widely available, aftermarket support is extensive, and the engine's straightforward design means many routine maintenance jobs can be handled without specialized     tools or advanced mechanical experience. Those qualities have helped keep Evolution-powered Softails, Dynas, and Touring models built throughout the late 1980s and 1990s popular on the used market. For riders who value proven reliability over the latest technology, that's a compelling combination. Of course, no motorcycle is reliable simply because of the engine bolted into its frame. The newest Evolution-powered Harleys are now more than 25 years old, so overall condition matters just as much as the V-twin itself. A neglected bike with poor maintenance records, worn suspension, or aging electrical components can quickly erase the advantages of an otherwise dependable engine. A thick folder of     maintenance receipts is often worth more than a spotless chrome cover. Regular oil changes, charging system repairs, and evidence that the motorcycle has been ridden and cared for consistently usually tell you far more about its future reliability than an unusually low odometer reading. That long-term record is why the Evolution still earns the nod as Harley-Davidson's most reliable V-twin. The Milwaukee-Eight has already established itself as one of Harley-Davidson's most     capable engines. Whether it eventually surpasses the Evolution will depend less on engineering than on how it performs over the next several decades. Until then, the Evolution remains the benchmark every Harley-Davidson V-twin is measured against. We want to hear from you. title: In the battle of Elon Musk v the press, we can’t let truth be the loser | Jane Martinson - The Guardian
content: The trillionaire Tesla owner has called the editor of the Economist a ‘traitor to the west’ after a clash-filled interview. How should the media respond? Elon Musk’s long interview with the editor of the Economist is as good a representation as any of the current clash between two worlds. In one corner, the editor of an 182-year-old news organisation which promotes economic liberalism and freedom. In the other, the world’s first trillionaire, who spreads misinformation to his hundreds of millions of followers on his own social media platform. The bout is a masterclass in the challenges journalists face in a new world of AI, fact avoidance and online aggression. The flash points in Zanny Minton Beddoes’ conversation with Musk start with definitions. Musk says that the people Minton Beddoes calls “far-right” and “fringe” (she mentions Germany’s AfD party) are in fact just “normal people”. They clash over whether the speed of his cuts to USAID led to unnecessary deaths in developing countries – she believes his claim that it didn’t defies not only statistics but the evidence from her reporters on the ground. Asked if he is racist, he cites the fact he has four children with a woman who is “half Indian”. In an awkward exchange, when asked by Minton Beddoes whether he is anti-Muslim, Musk says he is against “people coming to a country with antithetical views … I’m against rape and murder.” The tone shifts when Minton Beddoes accuses Musk of spreading misinformation about Europe and particularly her home town, London, telling him that the statistics show that it is a safer place to live than most large US cities. She appears genuinely irritated that he rejects all evidence that violent crime is far lower than he says and grooming gangs are not terrorising the streets. After she asks if he understands why this makes people loathe him, it becomes a playground spat. Musk points out that with so many followers on X, he must be popular. Besides, “they hate you far more than they hate me”. She admits to the media losing trust. The exchange says a lot, not just about both participants and what they believe in, but also the state of our current media ecosystem. To use the metaphor of the summer, if the interview were a Homeric quest, the editor would be trying to get back to a place of truth and safety while Musk would be the angry sea god unleashing violent storms and monsters after the challenge was seemingly over. That dynamic was mirrored in the response. The interview appears to end with the two agreeing to disagree; they even continue to chat while Musk has his photo taken. When Minton Beddoes promoted the interview on X, Musk then reposted it, adding “zany interview with Zanny”. She liked this so much she reposted his repost. After some of his followers posted rude things about the media he piled in on “the reality distortion nightmare mirror that is the legacy mainstream press”. By the weekend, he was calling her a “traitor to the west”. On Thursday, she confessed to being “bemused” but not scared by the “more and more aggressive” response. She has learned not to look at online comments, she told Radio 4’s Media Show. “If you scroll through them and read hundreds of things saying how awful you are, it’s not very pleasant, so don’t do it.” It seems particularly timely to see what lessons can be learned from all this, given the latest government-backed investigation into the safety of journalists found that many admitted to self-censoring reports on contentious issues such as rightwing protest for fear of being attacked. Throwaway vitriolic comments about journalists are directly linked to increased aggression online and off, the report found. Female journalists bear the brunt of this aggression. The shift to online and video journalism, the increasing celebritification if you will, has made more journalists identifiable, and therefore afraid for their safety. Again, Minton Beddoes is a great example of this given that the Economist, famous for the anonymity of its writers, has recently moved into far more video content. The Insider – the platform on which she interviewed Musk – is a weekly interview launched last September; guests have included Benjamin Netanyahu and Tucker Carlson, so Minton Beddoes is no stranger to combative subjects. Musk’s view of truth is the reason the exchange feels more important than similar confrontations. Asking powerful people questions and continuing to try to find the answers even when they react badly is the essence of what journalism is. In her short response to newsletter subscribers this week, Minton Beddoes promised to double down on the issues raised in the interview. She told them to look forward to new reports examining the facts surrounding the impact of shutting down USAID, the number of victims of grooming gangs in Britain and the amount of violent crime in European cities – all topics she had clashed with Musk over. The news business has not always behaved as ethically as it should and trust levels are at an all-time low and falling across the developed world. But data and on-the-ground reporting are the only ways to beat misinformation. You can claim that it’s just too dangerous to walk around in Britain, as Musk did – despite having not visited for several years – or you can find the data which suggests that homicide rates in general and even knife violence crimes are far lower than in major US cities, as the Economist did in a social video liked 73,000 times. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more Ownership of his own platform and infinite riches may give Musk a loudspeaker, but this old-fashioned reporting is the kind of public service the world needs. Especially if Musk really is the Cassandra he says he is and artificial intelligence is going to best humans within a decade, making it even harder to keep a firm hold on reality. Jane Martinson is a Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group. title: Apalachicola’s V-shaped pier making a comeback years after Hurricane Michael - WJHG
content: APALACHICOLA, Fla. (WJHG/WECP) -Nestled where the Apalachicola River meets the bay, a beloved local fishing spot is finally making a comeback years after Hurricane Michael washed it away. Apalachicola’s iconic V-shaped pier is under reconstruction. Construction just wrapped up on Phase 1. “This is something that was very near and dear to Apalachicola’s heart for many years, and Hurricane Michael actually took out the pier back in 2018,” said John Solomon, the Franklin County TDC director. “The TDC has been working with the city of Apalachicola to get this pier rebuilt.” While the pier is not quite back to its V-shape yet, Phase 1 adds the Dr.John Gorrie Observation and Fishing Pier — 350 feet of pier along the side of the Apalachicola River. “It’s one of the first things you see as you come across the bridge into Apalachicola is this pier,” said Solomon, “to see it start to come back to like it was before — even better than it was before — it’s a great thing for the view for Apalachicola, and for our residents to be able to come and enjoy the nature that Apalachicola offers." The new pier is ADA compliant, featuring bump-outs designed for wheelchair users and children. According to Solomon, the Apalachicola River and the Bay meet at the pier. He says freshwater from the river mixes with the saltwater of Apalachicola Bay — creating a feeding ground for redfish and trout. Sturgeon can also be spotted passing through at times. If approved, Phase 2 would add 430 additional feet of pier bordering the city’s Battery Park Recreational Boat Marina. Phase 2 is expected to start in October and wrap up sometime in January. Phase 1 of the project was funded by a $500,000 grant from Franklin County’s Tourist Development Council. Phase 2 is also estimated at $500,000 and will also use TDC funds. title: How Trump v. Slaughter Strengthens the Case for Third-Party AI Regulation - lawfaremedia.org
content: The upcoming main navigation can be gotten through utilizing the tab key. Any buttons that open a sub navigation can be triggered by the space or enter key. The recent decision takes off the table one of the most popular proposals for AI governance: an independent federal agency, free from a president’s whims. In the world of artificial intelligence (AI) governance, important developments don’t always come with the words “artificial intelligence” attached to them. That was the case with last month’s decision in Trump v. Slaughter, in which the Supreme Court overruled a New Deal-era precedent and held that the president has the power to fire a federal trade commissioner to advance his policy priorities, despite a law limiting such removals. The case is sure to have widespread consequences for the federal government across the board, as removal protections have been part of the structure and politics of many independent agencies for decades. But it is likely to be particularly significant for a key challenge facing the country: developing effective, accountable governance of AI, which is both increasingly capable and increasingly integrated into the economy. Trump v. Slaughter takes off the table one of the most popular proposals for AI governance: an independent federal agency, run by a set of commissioners who cannot be removed at the president’s whim. In doing so, it leaves proponents of AI regulation with fewer options, forcing them to choose between direct regulation by a federal agency without political independence from the president or the greater independence offered by regimes that incorporate private third-party regulators. Meanwhile, the recent actions of the federal government provide many lessons for this debate—lessons that make additional layers of political insulation look more and more appealing. The result may be that, although the Slaughter majority aimed to restore presidential control over policy, the best response in the world of AI governance ends up being to diffuse some control to non-state actors while maintaining an ultimate accountability check in a federal oversight agency. The Case for Third-Party Regulation Before Slaughter Over the past few years, there has been a growing chorus of arguments in favor of incorporating third-party regulation into AI governance in some way. This could take a few forms: current significant visions include a variety of elements, such as a regime in which independent auditors assess companies’ own safety and security claims, or one in which the government sets standards and auditors evaluate companies’ compliance with those standards. Third-party auditing could be opt-in (in exchange, say, for liability limitations) or mandatory; auditors could compete in what Gillian Hadfield and Jack Clark call a “regulatory market” or be funded by the government. Why rely on these third parties at all, instead of just directly having the government regulate and audit AI developers? The standard arguments have focused primarily on two areas: speed and human capital. Regulating AI requires a system that can pay large amounts of money to hire scarce technical talent and that can pivot rapidly to address new types of concerns. Historically, government agencies struggle in both of those areas, operating on civil service pay scales and multiyear rulemaking cycles. It might be possible to adapt the federal agency model to fit the occasion, but that also might run afoul of the Supreme Court—as happened, for instance, with the Court’s rejection of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s independent solo director model. The case for third-party regulation is not a slam dunk. In particular, third-party regulation has serious principal-agent problems. To take one famous example, Esther Duflo and her co-authors found in a study in the Indian state of Gujarat that auditors chosen and paid by the firms they audited systematically underreported pollution. (In contrast, when auditors were instead randomly assigned, paid fixed fees from a common pool, and monitored better, their reporting increased in accuracy and pollution actually fell.) The U.S. financial system’s reliance on third-party credit rating agencies contributed to the financial crisis of 2008. Nongovernmental AI auditors raise serious concerns with safetywashing, where an ineffective auditor’s seal of approval helps developers appear safer than they really are. Some of these problems are well understood. But understanding them is not the same as solving them, especially because politics and capture will be at work during the regulatory design process itself. Nonetheless, a strong role for third parties in AI regulation is starting to gain traction. Just this week, Governor JB Pritzker signed legislation making Illinois the first state to require annual independent third-party audits of frontier AI developers’ safety practices, and Connecticut’s new AI law creates a pilot program for state-approved independent verification organizations to assess AI systems. These are still the early days of third-party involvement in AI governance. But these are still the early days of AI governance, period, and these recent bills are a testament to what policymakers think is a plausible direction. On top of the more common speed-and-flexibility arguments in favor of third-party regulation, the events of 2026 so far have raised the profile of another factor: political insulation. The past few months have highlighted some of the more negative possibilities that can come with direct involvement of political officials in the regulation of AI companies. First, in late February came Anthropic’s escapade with the Department of Defense. After Anthropic refused to agree to certain contract terms with the department, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth went nuclear, designating Anthropic a supply chain risk (an act typically reserved for foreign entities) and announcing that no company that does business with the U.S. military could “conduct any commercial activity with Anthropic.” These moves struck many as unlawful right off the bat and were enjoined by a federal court. Then, in mid-June, came the export controls issue with Fable and Mythos. Three days after Anthropic launched its most capable models yet, and after two months in which the company had engaged in a limited release and briefed and consulted the government, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ordered Anthropic to suspend access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 by any foreign national anywhere in the world. In practice, that forced Anthropic to cut off access to the models entirely. The Friday-evening directive, by Anthropic’s account, did not detail the underlying security concern. Within a few days, a large group of cybersecurity experts spoke out against the government’s actions, arguing that the government had undermined cybersecurity efforts without a compelling justification. Much has been written about these events, and not everything is cut-and-dried—there are clear reasons for the government to be concerned about the widespread release of tools that can lead to increased cyberattacks, for instance. But some aspects of these actions are troubling: They were unilateral and opaque, were delivered without published standards, and appear to be concentrated on one company even when direct competitors may be similarly situated. That is why Slaughter should be understood as arriving at a critical moment. The independent agency has at times been a leading institutional answer to exactly this problem. In the AI context, for instance, the bipartisan Blumenthal-Hawley framework proposed a licensing regime run by an “independent oversight body,” an idea industry leaders repeatedly endorsed before Congress in 2023. So this year has delivered a double whammy: The risks of direct political control of AI regulation have never been clearer, and one of the historical tools for mitigating those risks is now off the table. To be sure, agency independence was never perfect: If you want electoral accountability, you have to have elected officials oversee agencies in some way, which will always entangle politics and policy. But Slaughter eliminates an important way of fine-tuning the design of our policymaking institutions. How much can third-party regulatory frameworks help address the issue of political independence? After all, government control is both desirable and necessary. It’s desirable because there needs to be public accountability when it comes to governing an incredibly important industry that so far lacks a major regulatory framework. And it’s necessary because the Supreme Court has demonstrated that there are limits to the kinds of delegation and oversight arrangements it is willing to tolerate, including both the Slaughter case itself as well as at least some stirrings about the possible revival of the private nondelegation doctrine. It would therefore be a mistake to view third-party regulation as capable of achieving absolute independence, and also a mistake to view such independence as a worthwhile goal. But third-party regulation could have some features that create an insulating layer between executive action and AI governance. For one, political involvement in the third-party regulatory layer could be more intermittent, via grants or reviews of licenses, than the kind of daily direction of activity that you can get in a federal agency. Contracts or licenses awarded over longer time horizons could foster independence—although there are trade-offs there when it comes to public control, too. But an independent auditor whose leadership cannot be fired by letter on a Friday evening, or whose contract termination could be conditioned on a formal process, could provide at least a partial buffer when it comes to executive involvement in significant regulatory actions. Third-party organizations could also help with the public information environment around AI governance. As the events of this year have shown us, AI governance suffers from an opacity problem, both because of its technical complexity and because of its national security implications. It will often be easy for the executive branch to make an essentially unreviewable assertion that a particular model is unfit for release, hiding behind technical details or invoking confidentiality in ways that make it difficult for outsiders—even experts in civil society or Congress—to assess the claim. That is more or less what happened with Fable, where the public was left to adjudicate between the government’s undisclosed evidence and the company’s self-interested rebuttal. Third-party organizations won’t eliminate the need for the executive branch to perform national security reviews of AI technology. It seems both unlikely and imprudent for the government to farm that out. But independent organizations can mitigate the problems on display this summer in at least two ways. First, outside of surprises and genuine crises, there needs to be a day-to-day regulatory system for assessing the safety of developers’ operations and products—and locating that system outside the highly discretionary export controls process, with independent experts providing the default technical testing, will shrink the openings for politically motivated malfeasance, and will likely increase transparency. Second, independent auditors can provide an expert counterweight to the executive branch, supplying context for evaluating the executive’s claims and decisions. This will result in a more informed public, including civil society experts, elected officials, and the international community, in addition to everyday voters. The advantages of third-party regulation are not just a matter of giving AI developers more room to operate by restricting the government’s hands. Political insulation can be desirable even if you want a more robust regulatory apparatus than we have now. It is hard to know what market structure will exist for AI five or 10 years from now. But frontier AI has the potential makings of an industry built around a small number of “national champion”-style companies, with a handful of frontier developers responsible for an outsized share of market value, national prestige, and government contracts. In such a world, the motivations to play favorites and engage in quid pro quo regulatory dealmaking will be strong. That can result in what Luigi Zingales terms a “Medici vicious circle” in which market power buys political power, and political power leads to more market power. Today, the executive branch’s calculus leads it to come down harder on Anthropic; but tomorrow might involve bestowing unusual favors on Anthropic or one of its competitors. Independent auditors with longer time horizons can therefore be a good idea for those who want to make enforcement reliable, not just those who find today’s policy regime excessive. Getting the design right will require balancing all of these considerations, and whether the use of third-party regulators is the best option will depend on the details and the other options on the table. A badly built third-party regime could easily be worse than a well-structured public agency. But the Slaughter majority’s project of concentrating control in the president may, in this corner of the law, produce exactly the opposite response: a governance system that deliberately diffuses power outward, to third parties whose independence no longer has anywhere else to live.

title: 450,000 defrauded student loan borrowers are eligible for debt forgiveness — here's who qualifies - CNBC
content:
Hundreds of thousands of student loan borrowers have gotten their debts forgiven, or soon will, due to a $23 billion class-action settlement with the U.S. Department of Education. The student loan borrower plaintiffs said that their schools significantly misled them and that the Trump administration delayed delivering the relief to which they were entitled under a protection known as Borrower Defense. That program allows defrauded federal student borrowers to get their debt excused. In late July, a federal appeals court denied Trump officials’ latest request to postpone making a decision on a large swath of the applications, paving the way for another nearly 200,000 borrowers to get their student loans wiped. That brings the total number of borrowers to get their debts forgiven under the settlement to about 450,000. The legal challenge played out over three presidential terms, its name changing from Sweet v. DeVos to Sweet v. Cardona to Sweet v. McMahon. One student loan borrower’s debt swelled to roughly $400,000 from $250,000 while she waited for the Education Department to decide on her Borrower Defense claim, said Eileen Connor, the president and director of The Project on Predatory Student Lending, an advocacy group. PPSL brought the lawsuit against the Trump administration in 2019. “It makes clear that the federal government cannot simply disregard borrowers’ rights and its own legal obligations without consequence,” Connor said. The Education Department did not respond to a request for comment. In court documents from April, the Trump administration said it needed time to determine eligibility for relief among an “unexpectedly large” number of applicants that could lead to a “substantial windfall at taxpayer expense.” Dozens of schools were implicated in the Sweet settlement “for which the Department had significant evidence of institutional misconduct,” Connor said. Many of the schools, but not all, were for-profit institutions that are now shuttered. These colleges made false promises to student loan borrowers, including that their education would lead to stable careers, higher earnings and transferable credits, she said: “Instead, many were left with enormous debts, credentials employers did not respect, credits that would not transfer, and, in some cases, no degree at all.” People were denied mortgages and car financing because of their federal debts. Others delayed starting a family or postponed medical care, Connor added. “Borrowers also described panic attacks, anxiety, depression and years of being unable to plan for the future,” she said. Eligibility for the Sweet settlement is based on what school a borrower attended and when they submitted their Borrower Defense application, Connor said. “It is not something one can newly qualify for today,” she said. If you had a claim pending with the Education Department in Nov. 2022, you may be included in the settlement class. But the relief also reaches certain borrowers whose applications were denied between Dec. 2019 and Oct. 2020. You should be able to check when your Borrower Defense application was submitted at Studentaid.gov. The Education Department also notifies eligible borrowers. The settlement only impacts federal student loans, said higher education expert Mark Kantrowitz. “Private student loans do not qualify for Borrower Defense,” Kantrowitz said — though nearly two dozen states maintain a tuition recovery funds program if you attended a for-profit school that closed. The average federal student loan balance cleared under the settlement exceeded $48,000, Connor said. “Individual amounts vary significantly, however, and many borrowers received substantially more or less,” she added. Borrowers who were eligible for the settlement may also qualify for a refund for any previous payments made on their debt. The typical refund for borrowers eligible for one is over $15,000, Connor said. The deadline for a borrower’s relief also depends on the details of their case and on when they applied for loan forgiveness, Connor said. Under the terms of the settlement, the latest the Education Department can clear an eligible borrower’s debt is June 15, 2027, Connor said. You’re not required to make payments while you wait for the loan forgiveness. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. title: 'No merging - we'll take them on, rugby v cricket' - Yahoo Sports
content: Rugby might be England and Saracens hooker Jamie George's first love but cricket is still a regular part of his sporting life and career. It's why he and his club team-mates did not need much persuading to sign up for a rugby versus cricket T20 match against some of the County Championship's top professionals in August, to raise money for the Motor Neurone Disease Association. "We [Saracens] do play [cricket] - our warm-up [for] every rugby session - summer, winter, snowing, rain - is one hand, one bounce," George told BBC Radio Somerset. "The boys love it because they're mad-keen cricket fans." George will skipper 'Team Rugby' for the game on 19 August at the County Ground in Taunton, in a side that also includes current and former England internationals Owen Farrell, Elliot Daly, Ben Earl and Max Malins. Somerset captain Lewis Gregory will lead the opposition to tie in with his testimonial year, with Surrey and England's Jamie Overton and former Somerset all-rounder Peter Trego also on the teamsheet. George was in the stand at the County Ground for a T20 match earlier this season and bumped into Somerset all-rounder Tom Kohler-Cadmore, who was injured at the time, and the idea was touted. "I'm actually doing a testimonial year next year and I said the dream would be to play a game of cricket somewhere like this," George, who captained England during this summer's Nations Series, said. "[Kohler-Cadmore] said: 'Why don't we do it for Lewis' testimonial?' I thought it's an unbelievable opportunity." Back with his Saracens team, George instantly started pulling a side together. "We were out to dinner and within seconds we were coming up with a batting order," he said. "I suggested we should merge teams and they said 'no, we want to take them on', categorically rugby versus cricket." While George and his team-mates are not short of experience, with hundreds of international caps and English Prem games between them, on the cricket pitch it is, of course, a different story compared to their opponents. However, the rugby squad do have some experience to call upon. Daly represented Surrey as a teenager and played for England at age-grade level, while Earl similarly played for Kent as an under-15. "They're both very handy so at least we'll get some runs on the board and then we'll have to scramble around a bit," George, 35, said. As for what kind of player George will be? "Like a Daren Sammy [former West Indies T20 World Cup-winning captain] type role, I would not bowl and I'd bat at nine or 10 and just be there for morale," he said. "I'm an old man now but I used to play a lot of cricket back when I was at school." Gregory, who is Somerset's all-time leading T20 wicket-taker, is happy the game is being played on his turf rather than the other way around and in a rugby match. "A lot of our lads are excited to see the rugby boys in action and it will be nice to put them under a bit of pressure rather than it being in a rugby game, because that could be a little bit messy," he said. The decision to support the MND Association was also an easy one for both Gregory and George, with former players in both rugby and cricket having been diagnosed with the disease in recent years. MND is a neurological condition which affects the brain and spinal cord, and can affect a person's ability to talk, walk and breathe. Former England and Gloucestershire fast bowler David 'Syd' Lawrence died in 2025, having been diagnosed with MND the year previously. Doddie Weir, the former Scotland lock, died in 2022, six years after being diagnosed with MND, and having raised millions of pounds and awareness to combat the disease, while former Gloucester lock Ed Slater and former England captain Lewis Moody both live with MND. "It's a horrible disease and that's why the rugby and the cricket communities are very similar, there's a lot of crossover between the two," George said. "We look after our own and we want to try to do everything we can to raise as much awareness and hopefully find a cure."

title: PREVIEW | Birmingham City v FC Barcelona - fcbarcelona.com
content: The first friendly of the preseason is always an exciting moment. The FC Barcelona squad have been training for the last fortnight, first in Barcelona and for the last few days in England, and now the time has finally come to get some match practice in. It won't be a full-strength Barça because the players that featured at the World Cup have yet to report back for duty, but there are plenty of things to look forward to in this 8.45pm CEST kick-off (7.45pm local time). And there should be no problem getting to watch the game because it's being streamed live on both Barça Play and via the club's official YouTube channel. The venue is Birmingham's regular home ground, the 29,409 capacity St Andrew's (known since 2024 for sponsorship reasons as St. Andrew's @ Knighthead Park). It's changed a lot over the years, but essentially it's the same ground that the club has now used for an impressive 120 years. Formed in 1875 as Small Heath Alliance, the team that carries the name of the second biggest city in the United Kingdom have spent around half of their existence in the top flight. However, the last time they featured in the Premiership was 2011, meaning they are currently on their longest ever spell outside of the top division. Traditionally, the 'Blues' have lived in the shadow of their city rivals Aston Villa, and arguably also West Bromwich Albion. They have never won the league and were beaten both times they reached the FA Cup Final. Instead, their biggest honours came thanks to the League Cup, which they won both in 1963 and 2011. Under American ownership, and much publicity when American football legend Tom Brady acquired a stake in the club, Birmingham are rebuilding, having finished tenth in the Championship last season and aiming to go even higher in 2026-27. There's plenty to look out for in the current squad, from South Korean Seung-ho Paik, who came through La Masia and played at the last World Cup, to players with previous experience in Spanish football such as Aragon-born Carlos Vicente, formerly of Alavés, John Solís and Patrick Roberts, both former Girona players, and the latest arrival, Argentine Luis Vázquez, who spent the second half of last season at Getafe, scoring three goals. While Barça have only played a 'practice match' against Europa so far, Birmingham City are much further into their preseason schedule. Having already played and beaten Huddersfield Town, Solihull Moors, Burton Albion, Crewe Alexandra and Northampton Town, this is actually their last game before their competitive calendar starts. Barça and Birmingham first crossed paths way back in 1925, when they played two friendlies in the Catalan capital, with Barça winning both. The first competitive meeting came in the semi-finals of the old Inter-Cities Fairs Cup, which ended 4-4 on aggregate and required a playoff in the Swiss city of Basel, which Barça won thanks to goals from two club legends in Evaristo and Kubala. In the following edition of the same competition, Birmingham achieved the honour of becoming the first British team to ever reach a European final. Once again the opposition was Barça and after a 0-0 draw in England, the blaugrana lifted the trophy with a 4-1 win at Camp Nou. With the World Cup stars still absent, the game provides a perfect chance for Hansi Flick to test some of his up-and-coming players, many of whom are knocking on the door of the first team. Ebrima Tunkara, Ibrahim Diarra, Shane Kluivert, Brian Fariñas and Orian Goren are just some of the players that will be keen to impress the coach at St Andrews. Raphinha, who barely featured for Brazil this summer due to injury, reported back to work this week, but is unlikely to play a role so soon. But there is a good chance that we will get to see German signing Karim Adeyemi make his unofficial debut for his new club, while Héctor Fort is back from his loan year at Elche. It will also be a valuable chance to see how players like Gerard Martín and Marc Bernal, who weren't selected for Spain this summer, are shaping up ready for the new season.

title: Nauticam Unveils Housing for Canon EOS R6 V - DivePhotoGuide
content: Nauticam has released its new housing for the EOS R6 V. Canon’s first V-series camera, which was announced in May, is based around the same 32.5MP full-frame CMOS sensor found in the EOS R6 Mark III and has much in common with that camera despite having features aimed at serious videographers and content creators. Like the EOS R6 Mark III, the R6 V can record 7K/60p RAW Light, 7K/30p open gate, oversampled 4K/60p, and uncropped 4K/120p, but with the addition of a cooling fan, it is capable of much longer (or unlimited) recording times compared to the R6 Mark III. The NA-R6V housing is designed to provide the best possible shooting experience for filmmakers while maintaining compatibility with Nauticam’s full range of accessories—from wet lenses to monitor connectivity options. Important controls are ergonomically positioned next to the integrated handles, while the N120 port system accommodates both RF- and EF-mount lenses. HDMI 2.0/1.4 monitors and monitor/recorders are fully supported, working seamlessly with Nauticam’s monitor housings such as the new housing for Atomos Ninja TX, Ninja TX GO, and Ninja RAW. The company’s water-contact optics, such as the FCP-1, WWL-C, SMC-3, and CMC-2, are all compatible. Nauticam’s vacuum check and leak detection system comes pre-installed. Priced at $5,400, the NA-R6V is available from retailers such as Backscatter. When purchasing underwater photography equipment like the products mentioned in this article, please support DPG by supporting our retail partner—Backscatter.com. The Canon EOS R6 V is a compact, video-first full-frame hybrid built around a newly developed 32.5MP CMOS sensor. It records 7K 60p 12-bit RAW internally, 7K 30p Open Gate for full-sensor reframing, oversampled 4K up to 60p, and uncropped 4K 120p for slow motion, all backed by an internal cooling fan that keeps long clips rolling. There is no built-in viewfinder: the R6 V is designed to be shot on its rear screen or an external monitor, which makes the way it is housed and monitored underwater central to getting the shot. That video-first design is exactly why the R6 V belongs in a purpose-built underwater system. A 32.5MP sensor feeding 7K RAW and oversampled 4K resolves every imperfection in the water column and in the glass in front of it, and shooting without an eye-level finder means the operator depends on a bright, well-placed monitor and controls that fall to hand on a moving reef. The NA-R6V is engineered to deliver both. Resolution and dynamic range of this order demand optics designed for the job. Water is an unforgiving optical element, and a sensor recording 7K RAW will show softness, chromatic aberration, or a curved field that a lesser workflow would hide. The NA-R6V opens the R6 V to Nauticam's N120 port system and its family of premium water-contact optics, so the picture stays sharp corner to corner and the field of view is the one the scene actually needs. The NA-R6V is machined from solid aluminium, hard anodized, and depth rated to 100m. It arrives set up to dive: handles, stabilizing brackets, and the moisture alarm battery are pre-installed out of the box. Because the R6 V is a compact body, the housing is compact too, at 358mm wide, 201mm high, and 134mm deep and 2.96kg in air, yet it is engineered to sit neutrally buoyant in the water with the camera and battery inside, so the rig neither pulls down on your wrists nor floats away from the subject. Every control the R6 V shooter reaches for on a dive is placed within a finger's travel of the ergonomic MIL handles, which lock to the housing with a Rotary Housing Lock for a rigid, rattle-free platform even when loaded with monitors and lights. An AF-ON lever sits under the right thumb and a Playback lever under the left, so pulling focus and reviewing a take never means hunting for a button. A two-stage trigger drives smooth half-press focus and clean record activation. The standout is a patent-pending dual-function lens control knob that handles both zoom and focus from a single wheel, switched between the two by a lever directly below it, which keeps power-zoom and manual-focus RF lenses fully controllable without cluttering the housing with duplicate gears. The NA-R6V uses the N120 Auto Lock Port System II (international patent pending), which seats and locks the port with a positive, tool-free action and drives RF lenses through the RF Lens Gear System II. Beyond conventional dome and macro ports, the N120 system opens the door to Nauticam's premium water-contact optics: the WACP-2 delivers a 140-degree field of view with compatible 14mm lenses, the FCP reaches 170 degrees with compatible 28mm lenses, and the WWL family and WACP-1B give wide, edge-to-edge scenes with near-zero minimum focus distance. For the small end, the SMC and CMC super-macro converters and the Mid-range Focus Optimizer let the R6 V's autofocus and resolution work at magnifications and working distances a bare lens cannot reach. Refer to the N120 RF Mount II Port Chart (C50 / R6III / R6V) for the full lens, gear, and port combinations. Because the R6 V has no built-in viewfinder, monitoring is not an accessory on this system, it is the primary interface. The NA-R6V routes the camera's full-size HDMI signal through a bulkhead to an external monitor housing, supporting both HDMI 1.4 and HDMI 2.0 cable systems. That opens up Nauticam's monitor and recorder housings, from the Atomos Ninja V and Ninja TX housings for 4Kp60 10-bit recording, to the Shinobi II housing for a lightweight bright monitor, to the 7-inch G7 and T7 UltraHD monitors for a large, gradable image on the reef. Purpose-built cables and M24 or M16 bulkhead options are available for each configuration. Sustained 7K RAW capture is demanding on the camera's battery. The NA-R6V accepts an optional USB-C bulkhead so a surface USB-PD power bank can feed the camera through the housing, extending record time well beyond the internal battery for long-format work and locked-off cinema setups. The NA-R6V is a video-focused housing: flash triggering and X-sync for still shooting are not supported. Underwater cinematographers light with continuous video lights, and the housing provides an extensive set of mounting points for them, including sixteen 1/4-20 UNC points and an M10 thread on the front top for mounting balls, plus three 1/4-20 UNC points and six M5 points on the base for tripod plates, skids, and strobe mounting balls. The NA-R6V ships with a built-in moisture alarm and leak detector, powered by a pre-installed CR-2032 battery, that warns of water intrusion before it reaches the camera. Paired with the optional 25625 M16 Vacuum Valve II, the housing also monitors the vacuum seal, confirming a watertight assembly on the boat and holding that assurance through the dive. The electronics are temperature compensated, so a warming camera or changing water temperature will not set off a false alarm. Part numbers below link to each item on nauticam.com. title: 🎥 Corinthians v Athletico: refereeing, injuries, no goals - Yahoo Sports
content: No goals at Neo Química Arena in Thursday’s (30) Corinthians vs. Athletico clash. With some confusing refereeing from Paulo César Zanovelli da Silva and few genuine scoring chances, the 0-0 scoreline held until the end. The match was part of the 21st round of the 2026 Brasileirão. A (negative) highlight was the likely serious injuries to Yuri Alberto — who had been rested — and Labyad. The first half featured a Corinthians side with more possession and attacking volume. Athletico — who rotated less with the Copa do Brasil in mind — did threaten first, in the 12th minute. But they did not force Hugo Souza into any major saves before halftime. The best chance fell to Diniz’s team. But Santos twice played the villain. Labyad had to be substituted before the end of the first half with a suspected sprain in his left knee. Diniz started using more regular starters in the second half. And one of them, Yuri Alberto, stayed on the field for only 29 minutes. He had to be substituted after a likely injury to his right thigh. Brasileirão top scorer Viveros nearly celebrated in the 27th minute when he rattled the crossbar. And in the 35th, he nearly pulled off the pass he had envisioned. Complaints from both sides about the referee marked much of the second half. Both teams did try. But a lack of sharpness on both sides prevailed. Corinthians moved to 29 points. They are eighth in the table. Both teams now turn their focus to the Copa do Brasil round of 16. Timão will visit Inter on Sunday (2) and then host them on Thursday (6). Meanwhile, Furacão will host Vitória on Monday (3) before heading to Barradão on Thursday (6).
